subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 21, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Coote.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not inclined to favour the amendment moved yesterday by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). We have to-day a tariff board set up for the express purpose of examining into all applications for changes in tariff. We have been insistent and will continue to insist that no changes be made in the tariff until they are examined into and reported upon by that board. It would be a grave mistake on our part to begin now to make exceptions to that rule. If we should insist to-day on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) making certain reductions in the tariff without reference to the board, where would we be if some future Minister of Finance taken from the other side of the House should begin to make increases in the tariff without reference to the board? What could we say to him? We would rot have a leg to stand on.
I am opposed to the amendment for another reason. I do not consider it good strategy. It may be a spectacular thing; it may be a heroic thing to undertake to demolish a fortress with a spattering fire of musketry, but it will not get one very far. I think Napoleon's great rule of warfare was: Always be stronger than the enemy at the point of attack. But the proposed amendment of my hon. friend reverses that rule and proposes to attack the tariff where it is strongest, to attack it at the point where it increases the cost of living. If he had undertaken to direct his attack at the point where it increases the cost of production, I think he could have made out a stronger case. I had the matter very aptly put in a letter which I received not long ago from a friend who said, The Canadian industrial coach is well able to bear the burden of taxation if you put the load on the axle where it belongs; but if you put the load on the tops of the wheels, it will act as a brake and tend to stop the coach. To my mind the greatest evil of the tariff to-day is that it puts the weight of taxation on the tops of the wheels and retards industrial progress. That is the point at which we should attack it. For these
reasons I say I am not in sympathy with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod.
Perhaps the most notable feature of the budget is the complete absence of any changes in the tariff. All things considered, I believe this was a wise plan. The tariff board is now functioning. It is bringing to light much valuable information in regard to the tariff which has not hitherto been available, and because of the existence of the board we are learning many things about the tariff which we never knew before. It is the part of wisdom that we should wait for the findings of the board' before attempting to interfere with the tariff, for the most outstanding fact that has been revealed in the discussions before the board is this, that no changes, either upwards or downwards, can be made in the tariff, the effects of which changes can be confined to any one industry, but every such change will be felt by every industry in the country.
It is imperative that before we undertake to make any changes in the tariff we have the report of the board as to just how far-reaching those changes will be. Some men have argued that the board has already reported on a number of cases, and they ask: "Why does the government not act in regard to these cases?" The answer is very simple. It is true that the board has reported on some twelve or thirteen cases, but those reports have only recently been handed to the Minister of Finance. They have not yet reached members of this House. Any changes made in the tariff and based on these reports will have to be decided upon by this House. The tariff advisory board gathers the information and submits it to the minister. Based on that information, the minister will make recommendations to the House, but we the members of this House are the men who will have to decide whether or not those changes are to become law. We are the men who will have to defend those changes before the people of the country, and I for one do not purpose going before the electorate and defending any change in the tariff either upward or downward by saying: "We made this change because the minister recommended it on certain evidence that he received from the tariff board, but what it was, I do not know." Before we undertake to sanction or to make any changes in the tariff we must have before us the reports of the board and the evidence on which those reports are based. It would cost the government a little more money, I know, to print the evidence, but they have already gone to considerable expense in creating the board to gather this

The Budget-Mr. Young (Weybum)
information, and of keeping a Hansard reporter there to record the evidence, and the only additional expense would be the cost of printing and distributing the report to the members. To-day we are in receipt of printed copies of all the evidence taken before the Senate divorce committee. Nobody reads it: we all throw it into the waste paper basket as soon as we receive it. That is a service that could very well be dispensed with, and the money thus saved could be devoted to the cost of printing the evidence taken before the tariff board and putting it into the hands of the members of this House.
But while it is important that we refrain from making changes in the tariff until such time as we have these reports before us, it is of infinitely more importance that we see to it that nobody else makes any changes in our tariff without our knowledge and consent. It is infinitely more important that we so frame our tariff laws that no man or body of men other than this House shall have power to say what our tariff shall be. I wish to call attention for a moment to section 47 (a) of the Customs Act, which reads as follows:
If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council on a report from the Minister of Customs and Excise, that natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada, either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers, the Governor in Council may, in any case or class of cases, authorize the minister to value such goods for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of this act, and the value so determined shall he held to be the fair market value thereof. *
That is section 47 (a) of the Customs Act. In a word, it gives the Minister of Customs and Excise power to place an arbitrary valuation on certain classes of goods if, in his opinion, the importation of those goods is injurious to Canadian interests. I ask you to pause for just a moment to consider the full significance of these innocent sounding words. Let me read them again:
If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council on a report from the Minister of Customs and Excise, that natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada, either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers

Last session I sat in this House day after day, week after week and month after month, from January to July, listening to hon. gentlemen opposite argue that all such importations were injurious to Canadian producers. Now let us suppose for a moment something that actually happened. Let us suppose that hon.

gentlemen opposite, who hold those views were to get into power, which they did, how hard would it be to persuade a minister chosen from their ranks that such importations were injurious to Canadian producers. All that it would be necessary to do would be to produce a customs return showing that imports were being made, and then what would follow? Read what the act says:
The Governor in Council may, in any case or class of cases, authorize the minister to value such goods for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of this act.
In other words, the Minister of Customs is there given power to set aside the whole Customs Act and place the tariff as high as he likes. Those are the provisions of section 47a of the Canadian Customs Act, and that clause was inserted by the parliament of Canada in the session of 1922. Was there ever sulch an abject surrender of the powers of parliament? Parliament when it inserted that section in the act practically said to the minister: We are no longer capable of managing our own affairs; we are no longer worthy to be free; do you manage our affairs for us, and do with us as you will.
I wish to call attention to another section of another act, section 6 of the customs tariff, commonly known as the Dumping Act. It reads as follows:
In the ease of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special duty (or dumping duty) equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof for home consumption; and such special duty (or dumping duty) shall be levied, collected and paid on such article, although it is not otherwise dutiable.
Provided that the said special duty shall not exceed fifteen per cent ad valorem in any case:
Then, further down, is a provision which says that such special duties shall not be imposed unless the Canadian producers are able to supply the market.
Now what happened. I have here a copy of order in council P.C. No. 1088, dated Government House, Ottawa, Tuesday, July 13, 1926, which reads as follows:

His Excellency
The Governor General in Council-
Whereas the Acting Minister of Customs and Excise reports that, from information in his possession, it is established that fruit and

The Budget-Mr. Young (Weybum)
vegetables of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada from glutted markets in the United States at values such as prejudicially or injuriously affect the interests of Canadian producers;
Therefore His Excellency the .Governor General in Council, under and in virtue of the provisions of section 47a of the Customs Act, is hereby pleased to authorize the Minister of Customs and Excise to value such fruit and vegetables for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of the Customs Act; the values so determined to be held to be the fair market value thereof.
So section 47a of the Customs Act was set in motion, and let us see what happened. The order in council was passed on the 13th day of July, 1926, and I have here a letter dated July 29, 1926, some sixteen days after, from a wholesale fruit and vegetable dealer, who says:
Under the authority of section 47a of the Customs Act and by order in council No. 1088 July 13th, the hon. the Acting Minister of Customs and Excise values certain fruit and vegetable products when imported from the United States of America, as follows:
Then he gives a long list of vegetables, and the valuations per pound-tomatoes, cucumbers, cabbage, celery, onions, potatoes, asparagus, carrots, beets, lettuce, spinach, cauliflower, peaches, raspberries, and, a few days later, pears, prunes and plums. The letter goes on:
The Canadian jobbing trade, as well as the consumer, is always willing to give preference to Canadian-grown fruits and vegetables at reasonable prices. In the past we have often passed up American goods at cheaper prices owing to certain help being needed in British Columbia. I have never known of vegetables being imported into western Canada when Canadian-grown vegetables were able to fill the demand. To-day-
That is sixteeen days after the order in council was passed.
To-day Ontario is not yet shipping tomatoes and British Columbia is unable to take care of the demand at $1.75 per crate, yet American tomatoes which on July 13th only cost around 50 cents a crate f.o.b. Tennessee are raised to a value of 85 cents a crate when they could do no harm to Canadian-grown tomatoes nor help the Canadian farmers, and is a straight tax on the consuming public. This means that all the customs would have collected would be 30 per cent of 50 cents-
The duty on tomatoes is 30 per cent:
-or 15 cepts a crate. There are 1,000 crates in a car, which would make the duty $150.
Under the new regulations, the duty is raised to thirty per cent of 85 cents plus fifteen per cent of 85 cents as penalty or a total of 38 cents a crate or an addition of $230 per car.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what was done? An order in council was issued giving the minister, under the authority contained in clause 47a of the Customs Act, power to place an
arbitrary valuation on tomatoes. He did so, and placed the value at 85 cents a crate when tomatoes were being bought in the United States for 50 cents. In so doing he raised the duty from 30 per cent of 50 cents, which is 15 cents, to 30 per cent of 85 cents, which is 254 cents. But the minister did not stop there. On top of all that he imposed the dumping duty. Section 47a of the Customs Act gives him power to put on an arbitrary valuation. Where did he get the power to impose the dumping duty? Not in the statutes of Canada. The dumping duty section specifically states that it shall not be imposed unless dumping is -being practised. That is to say unless goods are being sold for importation into Canada at a lower price than the price at which they are being sold in the country from which they -come, and the minister, after increasing the duty, turned round and imposed this dumping duty. What was the effect? The regulations under 47a and the order in council No. 1088, gave him power to increase the duty to 254 cents. If dumping had been going on he could have increased the duty 15 per -cent ad valorem. That would -have been at the very most 274 cents. He actually increased it to 384 cents. He actually increased the duty on tomatoes from 30 per cent to 764 per cent a straight increase of 464 per cent. How did he do it? He did it by pyramiding section 6 of the customs tariff on top of section 47a of the Customs Act. I inquired of the Customs department why that extra fifteen per cent was imposed, and they said that that was penalty. Penalty for what? Penalty for having an arbitrary valuation placed on your goods by the Customs department. Who gave the customs officials of this country authority to impose a penalty on anybody who was not violating the laws? They told me that dumping was going on. I undertook to find out whether it was going on or not and to find out what evidence there was that it was being practised. I went to the Minister of Customs and asked him. He reminded me that the Liberal party was not in power at the time and that the Conservatives were responsible. He referred me to his private secretary. I went to the private secretary and he referred me to the deputy minister. I went to the deputy minister and he referred me to somebody else. I went to that somebody else, and he referred me to still another. I think I went to every man in the customs building, except perhaps the policeman and the janitor, and I put the same questions to everyone. "What evidence had you that dumping was being practised last July when you imposed
542	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Young (Weybum)
the dumping duty?" They all made the same answer:	"Plenty of evidence", but when I
asked further: "Might I see the evidence?" they all began with one accord to explain that the evidence would be found in some other office. At last I found a man who told me he thought the evidence could be found in the Department of Agriculture. I wended my way to the Department of Agriculture and asked them if they had any evidence that dumping was carried on last July, and they said no, they had no evidence, but that they thought they knew where I could get it, and they put me in touch with the paid secretary of a growers' association who has an office in this city. I got the gentleman on the telephone and asked if he had any evidence that dumping was going on at the time referred to. He replied that he had abundant evidence. I said I would like to see it. We arranged an interview for the next morning. The next morning I screwed -my courage to the sticking point and went to interview in his own den, the man who dictates to the people of Canada what taxes they shall pay. He vas not such a formidable looking man when l met him, but was a very genial unassuming looking fellow, apparently quite unconscious of the power that he wields. He said, "You want some evidence of dumping", and I said "Yes", and he laid before me a number of resolutions passed by Canadian fruit growers associations in different parts of the country, asking that the duty be increased, on their products, I read them over carefully and I said, "These are very interesting, but you promised me some evidence of dumping", He said, "Oh, yes", and handed me a lengthy telegram from some marketing agent out in British Columbia, stating that the United States that year expected to harvest a very large crop of fruit, and Canadian growers were afraid that some of this fruit might find its way into the Canadian market, the telegram asked that the government take some steps to keep it out. I said, "This is very interesting, but you promised me some evidence of dumping". Now, Mr. Speaker, he had not one shred, not one scintilla of evidence of dumping. There was not even a charge of dumping, and finally he said, "We did not need any evidence, for we knew it was going on". That was enlightening. I then- asked him how he proceeded in the matter. The procedure, was very simple. He went to the Acting Minister of Agriculture. I am sorry that the acting minister has left his seat. The acting minister made representations to the Acting Minister of Customs-I am sony he is not in his seat. The Acting Minister of Customs made represent-

ations to his acting colleagues. I do not think any of them are in their seats. The acting colleagues got busy, and acted quickly in the matter. They passed order in council 1088 and all the rest was done automatically. How they arrived at the figure of 85 cents a crate as the fair market value of tomatoes in Tennessee last July, I do not know, and it makes no difference. Under section 47a as it stands, he could have placed a value of $85 a crate and still have been within the law. There is no limit. I think probably he arrived at S5 cents on the same kind of evidence as that on which he arrived at the fact that dumping was going on. It was John Bourinot who made himself famous by writing that book How Canada is Governed. I believe he could make himself famous in heaven if he would come back now and write the sequel to it. Let us review now briefly what happened. Certain tomato growers in Canada who were receiving a good price for their early varieties of tomatoes, but whose main crop was not yet ready for the market, being unable to supply the early market, and realizing that as soon as the main crop of Canadian tomatoes came on the market the price would drop, as it should drop, conceived the idea if they could shut out American tomatoes from the early Canadian market, they could store up Canadian appetites for their future use, and that by so doing, when the main Canadian product did come on the market the people would be so hungry for tomatoes that they would snap it up regardless of price. I do not know how wealthy these people are, but they are wealthy enough to keep a paid secretary in Ottawa to convey their wishes to the government. This secretary whispered into the friendly ear of a sympathetic government and section 47a of the Customs Act and the order in council passed under it did all the rest, and they increased the duty on tomatoes from 30 to 76i per cent.
My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), who was Acting Minister of Customs at the time, had much to say last session about the people defrauding the Customs department. I wonder if he will have anything to say this session about the Customs department defrauding the people when he himself was at the head of it. To-morrow, Mr. Speaker, I intend to move for a return showing in how many cases the Customs department has been compelled to disgorge the dumping duty after collecting it.
It used to be charged that our tariff was made behind closed doors, that certain giants of rapacity would call on the Minister of Finance in his office and tell him what they required in the way of tariff protection; and

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
it was done. The Liberal government a year ago undertook to put a stop to all this and appointed the tariff advisory board. Henceforth all applications for changes in the tariff were to be made before the board and heard in broad daylight, and were to be passed on by the tariff board before being submitted to parliament. But "what boots it at one door to make defence and at another to let in the foe?" No sooner had my hon. friends opposite got into power than they discovered a secret door through which the enemy could be admitted. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre, at that time Acting Minister of Customs and Excise, opened this side door, which is No. 47a, and allowed the enemy to come in. I am not arguing, Mr. Speaker, for a higher tariff, I am not arguing for a lower tariff; I am arguing for parliamentary control of the tariff. Under such an arrangement as this by invoking section 47a of the Customs Act in conjunction with clause 6 of the customs tariff, it is possible for officials to do anything they like with the tariff. I am arguing for a return to parliament of the power which rightfully belongs to it-power to say what our customs duties shall be. It was never contemplated that under the dumping clause the special duty should be more than 15 per cent, but by pyramiding one on top of the other they have actually put on a special duty of 46i per cent.
I urge on this House and on the government the necessity, first, of repealing section 47a of the Customs Act and, secondly, of making provision that the dumping clause shall never again be applied until satisfactory evidence has been produced before the tariff board that dumping actually exists.

Mr. Speaker, will the hon.
gentleman disclose the author of the letter that he has read *to the House?

The letter was
written by a wholesale dealer in western Canada, but I have not had time to get his permission to attach his name to it. However, the facts in it are all borne out by official documents to which my hon. friend can refer.

In the course of his remarks
my hon. friend asked a question which I should be very pleased to answer with his permission.

Yes, answer
anything.

The hon. member asked what effect this order in council had. In the riding
which I have the honour to represent it meant the immediate consumption of Canadian-grown produce by Canadian people.

I think we see
the effect before us.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. C. MATTHEWS (Toronto East Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask your indulgence for a brief space in order that I may make a few observations on the subject now before the House, namely, the budget speech delivered on Thursday last by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I congratulate the minister on his review of our financial position. His deliverance has the great merit of brevity and lucidity. To deal with the finances of Canada with such completeness in a brief address is in itself an achievement, and one upon which I have much pleasure in offering him my congratulations.
The minister takes credit for the present indications of a revival in trade and commerce. It is quite natural perhaps that he should do so. I do not know, however, that in assuming that credit the minister can lay claim to very much originality. If he inquires carefully he may find that other ministers of finance in their day have not been too modest to suggest at least that similar credit belonged to them. It is probably true there is a feeling of optimism abroad, but I am not able to follow the logic that this has been brought about by governmental achievement. Every banker, every publicist and every other man of practical knowledge of affairs, knows that through the efflux of * time and through much tribulation on the part of our trading and manufacturing community we as a country have happily emerged at last from post-war deflation; that stocks of merchandise have been liquidated and that the writing off period has finally passed. The great merchant class is now buying commodities, carefully it is true, but new and fresh stocks are in demand, not because this government has brought about the condition, but because the slow process of liquidation is virtually complete and a new demand for merchandise has at last sprung up. This is a condition to be desired, and is the inevitable consequence of drastic writing down and of the unprofitable era of trade through which we have recently passed.
Our deflation period was a long and trying one, longer than that of our neighbours to the south. Our early entry into the war, and our loss in manhood, which was high in comparison with that of the United States, made it impossible for us to have the quick recovery

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
which they enjoyed. That the tide has not really more than set in is shown by the current loans of our chartered banks. Their current loans and discounts at the end of December, 1926, amounted to $970,000,000; at the end of December, 1925, they amounted to $903,000,000-an increase of $67,000,000. This increase, so far as it is an indication, shows that there is some expansion in business, a little over seven per cent. But it is to be observed that the United States consular offices are still crowded with applicants who desire to leave the Dominion. Our savings deposits on December 31, 1926, amounted to $1,372,000,000, and our deposits not bearing interest to $608,000,000. With this general condition facing the Dominion, the resumption of business on a scale not experienced in recent years, was the sure effect of a certain cause, and only governmental action of an alarming nature could have prevented it. Added to this was the gratifying fact that the country in 1926 enjoyed a harvest of unusual quantity and value.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the question raised by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) in regard to the liquidation of our national debt. I approach this subject with a good deal of respect because it is of such magnitude and importance to Canada. I think you will agree that it should be dealt with in the most comprehensive and, at the same time, the most careful way. The minister was good enough to make a statement in regard to his prospect of handling the capital obligations of the country maturing in 1927. He pointed out that he hoped to be able to redeem the $8,000,000 four per cent three-year notes in cash, and he stated further in regard to the $29,000,000 five and a half per cent renewal loan maturing on November 1 of the current year that our finances permitting, he would redeem at least a portion of this loan in cash and the balance would be refunded. The loan of $63,000,000, five and a half per cent tax-free victory bonds, maturing on December 1, 1927, he will refund at a lower rate of interest, the minister presuming of course, that the present ease in money will continue until such time as he makes his refunding loan.
But the minister stopped at that point. He did not take the House into his confidence as to what his intentions are, if he has any intentions, in respect of loans maturing within a measurable period, and which are of great magnitude. The government may say that the time is not yet at hand for any particular worry or action in this regard, but I would respectfully point out that 
in recent months inquiries have been general concerning this matter. Surely it is not the intention of the government to wait until the year of maturity of these important loans to outline to the House and to the country what its intentions are.

A situation not altogether unlike this one, but of course of less magnitude, was found to exist three years ago in the province of Ontario. Not only were the annual deficits so large as to alarm the province, but the great bulk of the debt, which had been tremendously increased in recent years, was in a state somewhat similar to the condition of _ Canada's obligations of which I am now speaking. The then treasurer of the province, after consideration, decided to make a survey of the whole matter and he asked the Bankers' Association as well as the investment bankers to name an expert each. These gentlemen, together with the government accountant, made a survey of the whole debt of Ontario, with a view to its ultimate redemption, and they brought in proposals to retire the debt within forty years, which proposals the government adopted. tage to our whole financial fabric. The government also point with pride to certain reductions in taxation. This relief as far as it goes is welcome. Other countries are following the same course, and the reductions now proposed are only an indication of the general tendency of government finance. The income tax was instituted as a war measure in 1917. The war is over but the capital debt remains, and the ministry feels obliged to proceed with caution in doing away with this plan of taxation. Whether we agree or do not agree that Canada's income tax is a wise and necessary form of extraction, there are one or two facts upon which there should not be much difference of opinion. The first one is, that if this tax is to remain it should be enforced. The act makes it obligatory upon certain persons to pay taxes. Every resident of Canada to whom its provisions apply should be under the necessity of complying with this act. The enforcement should make every citizen who is assessable contribute his share as laid down by the statute. If latitude is allowed to individual discretion it would seem that the revenues must suffer in consequence. Is it reasonable to suppose that all taxable persons on April 30 of every year will make to the government a full and complete statement of all items of income received from any source for the prior year ending December 31? If it is an assured fact that without exception those assessable will do so, well and good, but I do not know of any country where such scrupulous care would be used by the population who are called upon to perform what many describe as a very disagreeable function, that of paying taxes. Perhaps we can learn, in this as in other matters, something from Great Britain where many years of experience with the income tax has taught them not to leave this matter largely in the hands of those who are to pay income taxes, but to collect at the source. This withholding of the tax at the instance of the government assures the country
The Budget-Mr. Matthews

of its proper collection, and all persons are treated alike in so far as they are involved in the necessity of contributing to the government's finances in this way. The tax is made compulsory and evasion is practically impossible. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am well aware that in many respects, as for instance in the case of the salaried man, and company directors and the shareholders, there is compulsion in Canada perhaps equal to that in England or in the United States, but in its broader application the tax is left in a large measure to the honesty of those making the returns. This is not a phase of the subject that one can reason to definite or accurate conclusions to be expressed in dollars and cents, but, nevertheless, one does feel that if there were no escape from the payment by those properly assessable the rates would not be as high as they are to-day to ensure the amount of money that is now collected.

If this is true, if the tax lacks universal application, that application should either be put into force or the tax done away with. Canadians should be treated alike. Dr. J. C. Hemmeon of the Department of Economics of McGill university, speaking before the Professional Institute of the Civil Service in Ottawa last night, is reported in the Journal to have said:
It is a little strange, that when our income tax was the same as the United States', they raised thirty times as much from this tax as we did in Canada.
Moreover, in the United States, all municipal bonds, or debentures as we call them in this country, are exempt from federal taxation. What the total of such securities would be, I have no idea; it would be a very difficult thing to calculate; but certainly it runs into the billions, and all those securities issued anywhere in the United States are, I understand, free from federal income tax. Canada has the advantage in that incomes received from all bond or debenture issues are taxable with the exception of those received from several federal bond issues Which will mature within the next ten years.
In the second place, if the tax is to remain, the rates should be lowered. In comparison with other countries and particularly with our neighbour, the United States, our rates of taxation on medium incomes are very excessive. The adjustment of -rates in 1926 had the effect of increasing the exemption and lowering the tax on comparatively small incomes. The particular point- that I wish to make is that a general decrease in the income tax schedule and the enforcement of the provisions of the act, wtould not necessarily involve a diminution in the amount of money received. Rates would be lower, and >if the tax were collected at the source, every taxpayer would be treated the same as every other, according to his responsibility. I am sure the government would be surprised at the happy results to the federal treasury.
As an example of this, it is well known to the Minister of Finance that the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States made in 1926 very substantial reduction in income tax rates, on the assumption that a scientific revision would not only result in satisfaction to the people, but would induce many who had exercised every possible device to escape income tax, to change their attitude when they found that ithe government had made drastic reductions. They would discontinue evasion and make pajrments according to the revised provisions.

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
So, it was with very special interest that the outcome of Mr. Mellon's experiment was awaited, and on January 26, 1927, the results were announced. These proved that, as a prophet, the Secretary of the Treasury had been vindicated. The collections for the year increased from $1,825,000,000 in 1925 to $2,172,000,000 in 1926, although the rates of income tax had been substantially reduced. There are those who are always ready to say that if you reduce our very high income tax rates, you will necessarily reduce the amount Collected. The experiment in the United States has not justified such a belief. On the contrary, it has shown that as a result of the very drastic reduction made prior to the collection of 1926 taxes, $346,000,000 more was paid in income tax money in 1926 than in 1925. This, in the face of the reduction in rates by congress early last year, was considered to be a most remarkable result.
The Secretary of the Treasury had told congress, and had emphasized the fact, that within reasonable limits reduced rates upon scientific lines would produce greater revenue. If levies were cut down to a sensible, peacetime basis, the tendency to evade taxation would diminish and the result would be increased income to the government. The figures completely support that theory, and so, Mr. Speaker, I venture to say that the same result could be achieved in this country. If evasions were stopped and if the rates were reduced, you would find surprising results and a more general approval of this particular tax, because every man would feel that he and his neighbour were both obligated to pay according to the amount of income they received.
There is just one other matter to which I would like to refer, and that is relief from income taxes of those public-spirited citizens who are giving of their means for carrying on work to the advantage of those who are less fortunate financially and who need either government or private assistance. Such relief, it seems to me, might well be instituted to the extent of contributions to hospitals and educational institutions. This country should not be able to afford to place a specific fine on largeness of heart. There are thousands of our citizens who are in need of hospital treatment and who cannot pay for it, and their good-hearted neighbours are coming forward and placing at the disposal of hospitals and other institutions funds that make it possible for them to help the poor and needy. In some cases gifts are withheld or diminished in size because of dissatisfaction over the application of the income tax to such gifts. On this account it is becoming more difficult

to realize from taxpayers the necessary amounts to carry on educational and charitable work.

My hon. friend! says, " because the people who paid it put up a holler," and I am inclined to agree with her. If I read history aright, I know this, that when income fax was imposed in any country it was imposed at its inception as an emergency measure. But I also know this, that wherever an income tax has been imposed upon a country, at no time in the history of that country, so far as I know, has the tax been entirely abolished. At times it is reduced, as the circumstances of the country warrant, but there is no country that I know of in the world to-day where the income tax has been abolished in its entirety after having once been put upon the statute book. Let me read something that was written iby an acknowledged authority sixty years ago, but which is just as opposite today. I am quoting from John Stuart Mills' Political Economy:
The only case in which a mere principle of political economy protecting duties can be defensible is when they are imposed "temporarily" (especially in a young and rising nation) in hope ol naturalising a foreign industry in itself perfectly suitable to the circumstances of the country. The superiority of one country over another in a branch of production often arises only from having begun it sooner. There may be no inherent advantage on one part or disadvantage on the other but only a present superiority of acquired skill and experience. A country which lias this skill and experience yet to acquire may in other respects be better adapted to the production than those which were earlier in the field.
But it cannot be expected that individuals should at their own risk or rather to their certain loss introduce a new manufacture and bear the burden of carrying it on until the producers have been educated up to the level of those with whom the processes are traditional. A protecting duty continued for a reasonable time will sometimes be the least inconvenient mode in which a nation can tax itself for the support of such an experiment. But the protection should be confined to eases in which there is good ground of assurance

The Liberal-Progressive members of this House are pledged to the reduction of the tariff in order to cheapen living and enable primary production to be profitably pursued. They are pledged to the maintenance of a reasonable measure of direet -taxation, based on ability to pay, through the medium of the income tax. They cannot but regard the apparent reversal of this dual policy in the budget of 1927 with misgivings and dissatisfaction. The reasons given by the government for the omission from the budget of a further instalment of tariff reduction may have, however, a sound basis in fact. The tariff board is at work. It is compiling information on many of the most important, and incidentally the most highly protected, Canadian industries. With the complete information at its command the government will be in a position to pursue the ]>olicy of tariff reduction. But, in view of the circumstances attending our

election, we must be absolutely confident that this pursuit is (the intention and policy of the government. body; but why should we not do as the people of the United States are doing? They have made their nation great simply by protecting their industrial population.
What did they do last year? Let me give the House one little instance. In 1925, we sent $1,400,000 worth of butter across the line to the United States side. The United States farmers immediately said: That is too much butter to be imported; we want greater protection. The United States government imposed an additional duty of four cents a pound on butter so that if butter went into 'the United States from Canada, it had to pay a duty of twelve cents a pound. Last year our export of butter to the United States amounted to only $101,000 worth, so that we lost the sale of $1,300,000 worth of butter to that country. Our good friends -and good men they are-from the prairies, that country of wide horizons and sometimes, I think, of narrow visions, although I do not know why, want free trade. There is no reason Why even if these gentlemen are penalized because of our protective tariff, we cannot repay them in some other way by subventions or by lowering railway rates, because I should not like to see our protective tariff bear unfairly on any part of this great Dominion. But we must do something to stem this tide of Canadian people going across to the United States. The people of the United States are laughing at us. From time back as far as I can remember they came here; they took our money; they would dump their goods on us. I remember when there was practically no money in that part of Ontario in which I lived. As an example to show how money was valued then, I remember a man telling this story, although I will not vouch for the truth of it. Having pulled a fifty cent piece out of his pocket-he must

I think I have pretty well run the gamut of what I intended to say. That is all we want. Let us build up an industrial Canada. Let us make of this a country in which our boys and girls who are educated on the farm will have some place to go. Last year a hundred thousand people left this country to go across to the United States and at least two thousand more I know left British Columbia without the immigration authorities having any knowledge of their going. It is no trouble at all for Canadians to step across the line and become residents of the United States. Mr. Speaker, in common with all members of the House I rejoice with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that he has been able to present to the House a financial statement which provides for a reduction in the national debt of some $31,000,000. I might add that I rejoice with the citizens of this country that in spite of the somewhat hectic session that was held in this House last year, the producers of this country, while the legislators were concerned perhaps more with party matters, were so intent on making Canada prosperous that the Minister of Finance is able to present the splendid financial statement he gave to us the other day.
The hon. Minister of Finance was very modest in claiming but little credit for governmental activity in producing a balance on the right side of the ledger. He attributed, as is nearly always the case, a great part of the 
credit to the splendid crops we have had in this Dominion. He also said that there was more of a buoyant spirit evident throughout Canada to-day than there had been at any time previous. I wish to develop that thought a little.
I believe that to-day in Canada there is more of a buoyant spirit, more of a determination on the part of our citizens to see that our heritage as citizens shall be guarded, rather than our heritage as partisans, and I am pleased that that is true. It has been quite evident since this House assembled that there is a desire on the part of the members to assist in a constructive way the legislation that is brought down. It has been our privilege to listen to the financial critic of the official opposition, and I have never before in this House heard criticism of such a constructive nature as was offered by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). I congratulate him upon his speech the other day.
But there are other contributing factors to the present prosperity of this Dominion which have not been touched upon at all as yet since this debate began. It is true that the crop of 1925 is reflected in the receipts and revenues of this country this year. It is true that when more wealth is produced, the artisans, tradesmen, labourers and farmers generally throughout this country have a larger purchasing power, which is reflected in the revenues of this country, because our taxation is based upon the expenditures of the people; in other words, our taxes are applied nearly every time that we make a purchase, and if the purchasing power of the individual citizen is increased, that is reflected in the country's revenues.
One very great factor in the increased wealth of this country, in my opinion, has been the organization and development of the wheat pool in western Canada, To that perhaps more than to anything else has been due the increased purchasing power of the farmers of Canada. We produce in this country, as was stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) the great majority of our exports from the soil, and wheat is the one commodity above all others which is exported in great volume. By organization the farmers of western Canada have been able to market in an orderly manner the bulk of the wheat crop of that vast wheat-producing area. In the crop year just ended, the amount marketed by the wheat pool of western Canada was over 52 per cent of the entire crop- over 187,000,000 bushels. By controlling the marketing of that vast quantity of grain, and

Not only has the price of wheat been raised to the grower, but wheat being the stable commodity, the staff of life, its increased price has had a beneficial influence on all othei' grains to a greater or less extent. Not only has the wheat pool had an influence on the price of wheat in western Canada, but it has maintained the price of wheat in eastern Canada, in sympathy with the price in the west, to a level in the fall of the year, at harvest time, that we never reached before in the history of the province of Ontario except in war years.
Analysing the balance of trade for the last few years, we find that it has a direct relation to the production of wheat in the western provinces. If the production of wheat in the western provinces is large and the return from that crop to the farmer is good, we find that that is reflected in the following year in the financial statement that is brought down to this House. That is the case this year. The balance of trade for the year 192526 was $402,000,000 in our favour, and that balance of trade bears a direct ratio to the splendid crop and the price obtained for that crop in western Canada. While I am from the province of Ontario in eastern Canada, I cannot help but recognize the great benefit that this organization has been, not only to the farmers of this Canada of ours, but to all business in Canada east and west.
I wish to come more directly to the budget and the items contained therein; but before dealing with this year's budget I wish
to make a few remarks upon the budget as presented last year. In that budget we had taxation reduction in two departments of collection, the income tax and the customs tariff tax. Outside of that no material reductions were made, and I wish to trace the effect of these reductions. The reduction that was made in the income tax last year produced a deficit, or a reduction in the revenue from that source, of $8,671,000; in other words, it had a direct adverse bearing upon the amount of taxes gathered from that source. Quite the reverse was the case in connection with the customs tariff. Although we had substantial reductions on some items, especially on automobiles and on lighting plants, the apparatus to generate electricity, and on a large number of other articles, yet our income from that source was increased $14,000,060, and I was quite pleased yesterday when the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), commenting upon a speech of an hon. member in this House, made the observation that tariff reduction always acted that way, that it always brought about an increase in revenue, and I was somewhat at a loss to know why the policy of reduction in the customs tariff was not followed this year rather than the policy of reduction of direct taxation. Reduction of income tax, as I said before, resulted in decreased revenue to the extent of nearly $9,000,000. Reductions in the customs tariff, although substantial in a number of instances, did not bring about decreased revenue; on the contrary, we have an increased revenue of $14,000,000. If the Minister of Finance was viewing this situation purely from the standpoint of the treasury and from the lesson which last year's budget teaches, surely we should have expected this session further reductions in the customs tariff, and, therefore, increases in the revenue next year. Quite the contrary, as hon. members well know, has been the course pursued, and that is why we in this comer of the House take exception to the budget as presented this year. I am reminded of a passage in Scripture which says:
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
And perhaps that may be so in this case. I was quite struck with the remarks of the hon. member who just addressed this House in his plea for higher tariff, for protection in this country, and I could not help observing that in the last fifty years our average tariff has never been below twenty per cent, and that it stands at over twenty-three per cent to-day. Yet under these circumstances the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Dickie) says we have lost hundreds and thousands of our Canadians to the great republic to the south. It might be well for us to look about for some other reason why our Canadians go to the south, rather than say that the lack of tariff protection drives them away. Surely, an average of twenty per cent assistance to industry, one-fifth, is large enough inducement, from the conservative viewpoint, to retain the citizens of this country within Canada. Should we not look for another reason? In my opinion the reason why hundreds and thousands are leaving Canada is that they are taxed out. A very good example of that was placed before me a few years ago, just before I came to this House, in conversation with a citizen of this country who had spent four years at the war. He said, "I hope the members of this parliament will try to reduce the customs tariff. You are taxing us out of the country. I returned from the war and got a job as a traveller. I found that travelling conditions were different from what they were before the war, and I had to have a car." This was before the reduction of the duty on motor cars was made. He continued, "A car costs me a hundred dollars more in Canada than had I decided to travel in the state of Michigan," which is just across the river from my county. "I had to furnish my office with typewriters and other equipment, and I found I had to pay nineteen dollars and some cents more than if I had decided to start travelling just across the river in the state of Michigan." He further added, "I am just as good a Canadian as ever stepped in shoe leather. I spent four years at the war, but you are taxing me out of this country." Now I want to place before the Minister of Finance, before the government and before the members of the official opposition this thought, that they may be induced to look at the real reason why the citizens of this country are leaving and going to the United States. It is true we are trying to check this exodus by an immigration policy which brings in settlers from Europe to go upon the land not only in eastern Canada but in western Canada. But to my mind as long as economic conditions are not what they should be in this country our immigration policy will not bring forth much fruit. The machine, so to speak, may work all right to bring the settler into the country, but unless we provide him the opportunity to gain a livelihood after he arrives
I-Mr. B. W. Fansher.]
here, that is, to make a profit on his farming operations, our immigration policy is not functioning properly. I might give a practical illustration in this regard, I think it has been given before. If the knotter on a farmer's binder is not tying the sheaves regularly he does not attempt to correct the fault by putting a new driver on the machine and telling him to go ahead. He corrects the fault at its source-he puts the tying apparatus in proper order. I want to say to the government and to the Minister of immigration that I do not think our system of immigration can be perfected simply by placing a new driver in the seat-even if he does come from the Progressive party. The trouble lies deeper. We must make the basis of agriculture fundamentally and economically sound. We must so shape conditions in this country that immigrants can make a living on the land, otherwise our immigration policy is largely in vain.
There are a few other items in the budget with which I wish to deal. The Minister of Finance has announced that by the reduction in the stamp tax on cheques, bills and notes, 70 per cent of the nuisance taxes will be removed. I agree with him that 70 per cent of the revenue will be lost; but 100 per cent of the niusance will remain. The nuisance is still there; every cheque over ten dollars, every note, every bill, must still bear a stamp. It is no more trouble to lick a 20-cent stamp than to lick a 2-cent stamp and place it on a cheque. The result of the reduction of the stamp tax on cheques is simply to throw away that much revenue without removing the nuisance. Very largely the only fellow who will benefit by the reduction is he who can write a $10,000 cheque. Hereafter he will pay no more than the man who writes a $10 or $15 cheque-the workingman. I cannot see that any equality of taxation is brought about by this reduction. Surely some persons othei than our labouring men got the ear of the Finance minister before he made this reduction.
The sales tax is a form of direct taxation, and is a tax which I do not object to at all. It costs the least to levy of perhaps any tax outside the income tax. The reduction of 20 per cent in the sales tax will afford some small relief to the labourer and the commonplace citizen, but outside of that I do not see that this budget will afford much relief to the ordinary Canadian. To my mind it gives relief to those of our citizens who are in the best position to pay. I regret this reduction because it comes at a time when we can ill afford to reduce this form of direct taxation.

The Budget-Mr. Fansher (Lambton)
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am criticising the budget because I am a strong believer in tariff reduction. I believe if, instead of this $27,000,000 relief which the Minister of Finance says the reduction in the income tax, the sales tax and the stamp tax represents, a similar loss in revenue had been occasioned by a reduction of the customs tariff, the relief to our taxpayers would represent at least $100,000,000. I base that statement on the fact that a four per cent sales tax on the business of the country is estimated in this budget to bring in $104,000,000 in revenue, while the average tariff tax which is 23 per cent on our business is estimated to bring in a revenue of only $141,000,000, although that tariff tax is five times as great in percentage. Therefore I am led to believe that the customs tariff is not nearly as efficient a method of collecting revenue as is the income tax. If we figure out the ratio, we Shall find that while one dollar is gathered into the. treasury three times as much goes into the pockets of the interests protected under the customs tariff. It seems to me that this perhaps is one reason why Canadian industry has not been as prosperous as it should be. I do not believe it is possible to build up a strong, virile industry by a system of coddling any more than it is possible to build up a sturdy manhood and womanhood by such a system. I think that industry can be made strong and prosperous in this country by being in large measure thrown on its own resources. Surely after fifty years of assistance under a protective tariff, under which our manufacturers have never got a lower average protection than 20 per cent, we may well urge a party that year after year has promised tariff reductions to give us results. True, in the fourteenth parliament some reduction was made on agricultural implements, and a further reduction was made last year. But it seems to me extraordinary conditions must develop before we can effect a reduction in the customs tariff. I hope however that the government realizes the importance of implementing this plank of their platform, which apparently they are abandoning,-a plank which, by the way, had a good deal to do with the election of a considerable number of those who sit to the right of the Speaker. The tariff reduction afforded in the last budget, and the promise of further reductions, played no small part in returning an increased Liberal membership from the province of Ontario. Just so long as the government keeps faith with those electors, just so long will they retain their confidence in the future.
There never was a time in the history of Canada when the people were so free from party ties, and so eager to approach every question from the broad standpoint of Canadian citizenship as a whole, as they are today, and governments may well take warning that promises made by political parties will be expected to be carried out to the letter. This is the case to-day more than ever before in our history.
There is no doubt that there has been an alarming exodus in the last twenty years. Out of over 400 townships in old Ontario only 61 have increased in population in that time, according to the 1921 census, and these few have been close to cities or towns where there has been an overflow into the township. In some constituencies there has been a reduction of 5,000 in ten years. The rural citizens believe that the foundation of any nation is the soil, and that is why they are anxious that tariff relief shall be given the agriculturists. This is what the rural communities of Ontario want, so that they may rebuild this old province. There is homestead after homestead throughout the province unoccupied at the present time, and vast pasture lands waiting to be utilized. We must not forget that the foundation of the nation is agriculture. It is time, therefore, that we harked back to the welfare of the men on the soil; otherwise we may wake up some day and find ourselves in a very unenviable situation. We are this year commemorating the diamond jubilee of Canadian confederation. We have been sixty years a nation. I trust that when the celebration takes place due consideration will be given the pioneers of this country, those who laid its foundations and handed down to us the great heritage which we enjoy. The agriculturists of Canada for fifty years have contributed to the welfare of Canadian industry to the tune of over twenty per cent, and it was sincerely to be hoped that in this jubilee year we might have expected a budget that would give a substantial measure of tariff relief to the rural communities.
